t: Reach End of Array With Max Score — Greedy Carrier
o: You start at index 0 and repeatedly jump to a larger index; a jump from i to j earns (j-i)*nums[i]. You must maximize the total score upon reaching the last index. In example [1,3,1,5], hopping to index 1 then to 3 gives 1*1 + 2*3 = 7, beating a direct jump worth 4. In [4,3,1,3,2] the first element dominates everything after it, so one direct jump gives 4*4 = 16. With n up to 1e5 we need at least an O(n log n) way of deciding where to stop; the key observation is that the answer decomposes into unit steps.
k: Each unit step from position i-1 to i is paid at the value of the 'carrier' position you last stopped at.
It is optimal to switch carriers exactly when a strictly larger value appears, because a larger carrier pays for all subsequent steps until superseded.

a.i: Define dp[i] as the maximum score to stand at index i. Every arrival at i comes from some earlier j, contributing dp[j] + (i-j)*nums[j]. Trying all predecessors is O(n^2) — fine conceptually, too slow for n = 1e5, but it validates the greedy.
s: For each i from 1 to n-1, set dp[i] = max over j < i of dp[j] + (i-j)*nums[j].
a.t: O(n^2) — every pair (j, i) is relaxed once.

a.i: Reframe the score as n-1 unit steps: moving one index right while your carrier is v pays v. Starting with carrier nums[0], whenever the incoming element is larger than the carrier, it is optimal to land there and adopt it as the new carrier — a bigger carrier can only help all future steps. Summing the carrier over every step gives the answer in one pass.
s: For i from 1 to n-1: add carrier to ans (the step into i is paid by the current carrier).
If nums[i] > carrier, update carrier = nums[i].
a.t: O(n) — a single pass with constant work per element.

w: Use the greedy in an interview; present the DP only to motivate it. Watch out for overflow: the answer can reach 1e5 * 1e5 = 1e10, so use 64-bit integers in C++/Java. Edge cases: n = 1 returns 0 (no jumps), and equal values never trigger a carrier switch (correctly, since switching gains nothing). Follow-ups: what if jumps could also move backward, or if each index could be used as a carrier only once?
